name: Rice bran extract
lead: Rice bran extract is a cosmetic and supplement ingredient derived from the bran layer of rice (Oryza sativa), the outer layer removed when brown rice is milled into white rice [14]. In skincare, especially K-beauty and J-beauty products, it is used for brightening, moisturizing and antioxidant effects, and people use it with the aim of a more even, luminous complexion [1].

The appearance chain is brightening: rice bran contains antioxidants such as ferulic acid, gamma-oryzanol, tocopherols and, in pigmented rice, anthocyanins [2][3][14], and in laboratory work a fermented extract reduced melanin-related signaling in mouse melanoma cells [4]. A safety review of rice-derived cosmetic ingredients covers their functions as skin-conditioning and occlusive agents [9]. No controlled human trial of topical rice bran extract for skin tone has been located; the Grokipedia article describes clinical results but is AI-generated and its citations were not independently verified [1].

Oral rice bran extract is studied separately: randomized trials have examined it in sleep disturbance, depressive symptoms and cardiovascular risk markers [11][12][13], and a 2025 review of herbal remedies for hair loss names rice bran extract among the agents it covers [10].

paras: Rice bran is the outer layer removed when brown rice is polished into white rice, making up roughly 8 to 10 percent of the paddy weight, according to Grokipedia [1]. It spoils quickly because of lipase activity, so it is stabilized, often by heat, before extraction [1].

Wikipedia describes the bran as a milling by-product rich in fiber, essential fatty acids, protein and minerals, with an oil fraction of about 12 to 13 percent, and notes constituents including tocotrienols (a form of vitamin E), gamma-oryzanol, beta-sitosterol and ferulic acid [14]. Its high oil content makes it prone to rancidity, so it is often heat-treated to extend shelf life [14].

Grokipedia reports that rice-washing water and rice bran powder (nuka) have been used for skin and hair care in Japan, China and elsewhere in Asia, with Japanese use said to date to the Heian period; it also describes a belief that sake brewers' hands stayed smooth and pale from handling rice [1]. These historical accounts come from an AI-generated source and were not checked against primary sources.

In Japan, rice bran is known as nuka and is used for pickling (nukazuke), for cooking bamboo shoots and for washing dishes, uses that sit alongside its place in traditional skin and hair care [14][1].
Modern formulations, including fermented extracts, feature in K-beauty and J-beauty lines [1].

Analyses of pigmented (black and red) rice brans found higher reducing power than a white rice bran extract, and the extracts inhibited lipid peroxidation in test systems [2]. Studies of Thai rice bran varieties likewise measured phenolic, flavonoid, tocopherol and gamma-oryzanol content and antioxidant activity in vitro [5].

In B16F1 mouse melanoma cells, fermented rice bran downregulated MITF expression and inhibited melanogenesis induced by alpha-MSH [4]. Black rice bran also reduced chemically induced inflammation in mouse skin [6].
No controlled human study of topical rice bran extract for skin brightening was found. The research on skin is laboratory and animal work described above.

Grokipedia reports that human studies of rice-derived formulations measured improved hydration and that a 10 percent black rice bran lotion reduced melanin and erythema within 14 days [1]; these statements were not verified against the original trials.

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 50 adults with sleep disturbance gave a rice bran extract supplement or placebo for two weeks and found, on polysomnography, shorter sleep latency, longer total sleep time and better sleep efficiency than placebo, with no serious adverse events reported [11].

A randomized trial of 100 adults with mild-to-moderate depressive symptoms compared an 8-week rice bran extract supplement with placebo and reported greater reductions in Korean Hamilton Depression Rating Scale scores in the rice bran group [12].

In a 6-month randomized trial of 60 postmenopausal Vietnamese women with high LDL cholesterol, a pre-germinated brown rice bran extract containing acylated steryl glucosides lowered LDL cholesterol and TNF-alpha relative to placebo [13]. Registered trials also address immunity and pharmacokinetics [7][8].

A 2025 review of herbal remedies for hair loss lists rice bran extract among the agents searched and concludes that natural remedies as a group show promise, citing mechanisms such as 5-alpha-reductase inhibition, blood flow and antioxidant effects [10].

A Cosmetic Ingredient Review report on rice-derived cosmetic ingredients found rice bran oil and waxes to be non-irritating in animal skin tests and rice bran oil not a sensitizer, and describes the ingredients as skin-conditioning and occlusive agents [9].
Grokipedia states that rice-derived cosmetic ingredients are generally considered to have low potential for irritation, allergenicity and phototoxicity in safety assessments [1].
Wikipedia notes that rice bran can contain inorganic arsenic and the antinutrient phytic acid [14].

card.summary: A K-beauty brightening botanical with antioxidant and cell-culture data but no controlled human skin-tone trial found.
card.aka: Oryza sativa bran extract, fermented rice bran, nuka
card.note: Human efficacy claims come largely from an AI-generated encyclopedia summary and lab studies.

quick.overview:
Rice bran extract comes from the outer layer of milled rice and appears in Asian skincare for brightening and hydration. Rice bran and rice water have a long history of traditional use.
Lab studies show antioxidant activity, and a fermented extract reduced melanin-pathway signaling in mouse cells. Controlled human trials for skin tone were not found.
quick.mechanism: Constituents such as ferulic acid, gamma-oryzanol and tocopherols act as antioxidants in test systems, and in melanoma cells a fermented extract lowered MITF, a regulator of melanin production.
quick.risks: Safety assessments summarized by Grokipedia describe low irritation potential at typical cosmetic concentrations; that summary was not independently verified.

chain: Fermented extract reduced melanogenesis signaling in cell studies
Aim of a brighter, more even-toned complexion
angle.text: Rice bran extract is used in brightening and moisturizing skincare in the hope of a more even and radiant skin tone. The supporting research is laboratory work on antioxidants and melanin signaling, plus the traditional use of rice bran powder and rice water in Asian skincare [1][2][4].
